claim: Exosomes from cells expressing both SBP-Flag-Cas9-GFP and Myc-streptavidin-CD63-mCherry were enriched in Cas9 protein.
source: Exosomes from cells expressing both fusion proteins were enriched in Cas9 and gRNA, whereas cells expressing Cas9 untethered to CD63 had little or no Cas9 or gRNA (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating Cas9-GFP protein detection in exosomes from cells expressing both constructs.

claim: Exosomes from cells expressing both SBP-Flag-Cas9-GFP and Myc-streptavidin-CD63-mCherry were enriched in gRNA.
source: Exosomes from cells expressing both fusion proteins were enriched in Cas9 and gRNA, whereas cells expressing Cas9 untethered to CD63 had little or no Cas9 or gRNA (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating ~15-fold enrichment of gRNA in exosomes from cells expressing both constructs.

claim: Cells expressing Cas9 untethered to CD63 had little or no Cas9 in exosomes.
source: Exosomes from cells expressing both fusion proteins were enriched in Cas9 and gRNA, whereas cells expressing Cas9 untethered to CD63 had little or no Cas9 or gRNA (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B showing absence of Cas9-GFP signal in exosomes from His-Flag-Cas9-GFP expressing cells.

claim: Cells expressing Cas9 untethered to CD63 had little or no gRNA in exosomes.
source: Exosomes from cells expressing both fusion proteins were enriched in Cas9 and gRNA, whereas cells expressing Cas9 untethered to CD63 had little or no Cas9 or gRNA (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1C showing minimal gRNA enrichment in exosomes from His-Flag-Cas9-GFP expressing cells.

claim: Cas9 and gRNA were sequestered within exosome vesicles.
source: Protease and nuclease protection experiments showed that Cas9 and the gRNA were both sequestered within vesicles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by protease protection assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and nuclease protection assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) showing protection of Cas9 and gRNA from degradation unless detergent is added.

claim: Expression of Cas9 protein in HEK293T cells with the reporter plasmid increased the Nluc/Fluc signal around 100-fold compared to control.
source: As a test, we expressed Cas9 protein in HEK293T cells with the reporter plasmid and found that expression of Cas9 increased the Nluc/Fluc signal around 100-fold compared to that transfected with control empty plasmid (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating dramatic increase in Nluc/Fluc ratio upon Cas9 expression.

claim: Exosomes secreted from donor cells increased the Nluc/Fluc ratio by only 50% at an excess of 10^5 exosomes per cell.
source: At an excess of exosomes/cell of 105/1, the Nluc/Fluc ratio increased by only 50%, markedly lower than the 70-fold increase in the ratio of reporter cells directly transfected with the Cas9/gRNA construct (Figure 1F) or co-transfected with both SBP-Cas9/gRNA and streptavidin-CD63 in the presence or absence of biotin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 1F showing minimal increase in Nluc/Fluc signal after exosome treatment compared to direct transfection.

claim: Direct transfection of reporter cells with Cas9/gRNA construct resulted in a 70-fold increase in the Nluc/Fluc ratio.
source: At an excess of exosomes/cell of 105/1, the Nluc/Fluc ratio increased by only 50%, markedly lower than the 70-fold increase in the ratio of reporter cells directly transfected with the Cas9/gRNA construct (Figure 1F) or co-transfected with both SBP-Cas9/gRNA and streptavidin-CD63 in the presence or absence of biotin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 1F showing SBP-Cas9-GFP plasmid transfection resulted in ~70-fold increase.

claim: Functional delivery of Cas9/gRNA from exosomes secreted by HEK293T cells was very inefficient.
source: Nonetheless, the signal was somewhat proportional to dose of exosomes (Figure 1G), but we concluded that functional delivery of Cas9/gRNA from exosomes secreted by HEK293T cells was very inefficient.
evidence: Based on comparison of exosome-mediated delivery (50% increase) versus direct transfection (70-fold increase) shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Similar inefficient exosome-mediated Cas9/gRNA delivery results have been reported elsewhere.
source: Similar experiments were performed using Cas9-enriched exosomes secreted by MDA-MB231 cells, and we found that these exosomes were also inefficient for the Cas9/gRNA delivery to MDA-MB231 cells as a reporter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F). Our findings were similar to those reported previously (de Jong et al., 2020; Haimovich et al., 2017; Somiya and Kuroda, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (de Jong et al., 2020; Haimovich et al., 2017; Somiya and Kuroda, 2021) reporting similar findings.

claim: Cas9-GFP from exosomes was internalized into U2OS cells and accumulated in intracellular puncta in ~30% of cells during a 16 hr incubation.
source: Tagged GFP antibody was used to detect internalized Cas9-GFP that accumulated in intracellular puncta in ~30% of the cells during a 16 hr incubation (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1H demonstrating intracellular GFP and CD63 puncta.

claim: Cas9 was internalized into cells but may not have been mobilized from vesicles to gain access to the luciferase reporter genes in the nucleus.
source: From these experiments, we concluded that Cas9 was internalized into cells but may not have been mobilized from vesicles to gain access to the luciferase reporter genes in the nucleus.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Cas9 was internalized (Figure 1H) but did not result in efficient gene editing (Figure 1F).

claim: Unfractionated conditioned medium from donor cells incubated with reporter cells for 3-8 days showed little change in the Nluc/Fluc signal.
source: Unfractionated conditioned medium from the donor cells was incubated with reporter cells for 3–8 days with little change in the Nluc/Fluc signal (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1I demonstrating minimal signal change with conditioned medium.

claim: Co-culture of donor and acceptor cells in a transwell chamber separated by a 0.45 μm pore membrane for 6 days showed no increase in Nluc/Fluc.
source: As a further test of vesicle stability, we incubated donor and acceptor cells in a transwell chamber separated by a 0.45 μm pore vesicle-permeable membrane. After a 6-day co-culture, no increase in the Nluc/Fluc was observed (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1I demonstrating no signal increase in transwell co-culture.

claim: Delivery of Cas9 is limited by inefficient fusion of exosomes with the endosomal membrane.
source: Therefore, we suggest delivery of Cas9 is limited by inefficient fusion of exosomes with the endosomal membrane (Figure 1J).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that exosomes are internalized but do not deliver functional Cas9, suggesting a fusion limitation.

claim: Substantial Nluc expression was observed in all donor-acceptor combinations except where HEK293T cells served as both donor and acceptor.
source: After a co-culture for 6 days to near confluence, we observed substantial Nluc expression in all combinations except where HEK293T cells served as both donor and acceptor (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating Nluc expression in various cell combinations.

claim: The highest level of Nluc expression (~60-fold increase in the Nluc/Fluc signal) was seen in co-culture of HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: The highest level of Nluc expression (~60-fold increase in the Nluc/Fluc signal) was seen in co-culture of HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating highest signal with HEK293T-MDA-MB-231 co-culture.

claim: There was little difference in the efficiency of transfer with CD63-tethered or free Cas9/gRNA.
source: Of note, we found little difference in the efficiency of transfer with CD63-tethered or free Cas9/gRNA.
evidence: Supported by comparison of different Cas9 constructs in Figure 2A showing similar transfer efficiency.

claim: Progressive transfer was observed over several days with a limit reached after day 3.
source: In a time-course experiment, we observed progressive transfer over several days with a limit reached after day 3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by time-course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A demonstrating increasing signal up to day 3.

claim: A gradual increase in signal was observed at higher levels of donor cells, but HEK293T cells serving as both donor and acceptor remained inactive even at a donor:acceptor ratio of 10:1.
source: On increase in the donor:acceptor cell ratio, we observed a gradual increase in the signal at a higher level of donor cell but HEK293T cells serving as both donor and acceptor remained inactive even at a donor:acceptor ratio of 10:1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C demonstrating ratio-dependent increase except for HEK293T-HEK293T pairs.

claim: After co-culture of HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells, double-positive cells were found indicating transfer of GFP fragments between cells.
source: After co-culture, doubl- positive cells were found (Figure 2C, bottom panel, Q2 and Q2-4 quadrants), suggesting transfer of one or both fragments of GFP between cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating cells with both GFP and mCherry or CFP signals.

claim: Transfer of GFP11 from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 occurred in around 6% of cells.
source: GFP+mCherry+/mCherry+ (Figure 2C, bottom panel) represented the ratio of cells with GFP+mCherry double-positive fluorescence, indicating a transfer of GFP11 from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 in around 6% of cells (Figure 2D and E, yellow bars).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 2D and E demonstrating ~6% double-positive cells.

claim: Transfer from MDA-MB-231 to HEK293T occurred in around 0.5% of cells.
source: GFP+CFP+/CFP+ (Figure 2C, bottom panel) represented the ratio of cells with GFP+CFP double-positive fluorescence indicating transfer from MDA-MB-231 to HEK293T in around 0.5% of cells (Figure 2D and E, green bars).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 2D and E demonstrating ~0.5% double-positive cells.

claim: No cargo transfer was seen when HEK293T cells served as both donor and acceptor.
source: As a control, HEK293T cells expressing CFP and CD63 fused 7*tandem GFP11 (Figure 2C, top panel) were co-cultured with HEK293T cells expressing mCherry and GFP1-10 (Figure 2F, top panel, P3 area). No cargo transfer was seen in this combination (Figure 2F, bottom panel, Q2 and Q2-4 quadrants).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F demonstrating absence of double-positive cells in Q2 and Q2-4 quadrants.

claim: Co-cultures of MDA-MB-231 as donor to several other tumor cell lines as acceptor (ratio of 10:1) resulted in cargo transfer to a limit of about 10% of cells.
source: Co-cultures of MDA-MB-231 as the donor to several other tumor cell lines as acceptor (ratio of 10:1) resulted in cargo transfer to a limit of about 10% of cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G demonstrating up to ~10% transfer to various tumor cell lines.

claim: Cargos were transferred from MDA-MB-231 to other cell lines, including the MDA-MB-231 cell line itself.
source: Of note, cargos were also transferred from MDA-MB-231 to other cell lines, including the MDA-MB-231 cell line itself (GFP+CFP+/CFP+ bars in Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G demonstrating transfer among MDA-MB-231 cells.

claim: Only 0.02% of acceptor cells reported GFP in the 12-24 hr incubation with exosomes, compared to ~6% in co-culture.
source: In contrast to the ~6% of cells that received GFP11 from donor cells in a 3–4-day co-culture, only 0.02% of acceptor cells reported GFP in the 12–24 hr incubation with exosomes (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of flow cytometry data showing dramatic difference between exosome treatment and co-culture.

claim: Delivery of exosome content may be limited by inefficient fusion to the endosomal membrane for exosomes produced by HEK293T and internalized by MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: These results reinforce the suggestion that the delivery of exosome content may be limited by inefficient fusion to the endosomal membrane at least for exosomes produced by HEK293T and internalized by MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that exosomes are internalized but deliver cargo very inefficiently (0.02% vs 6%).

claim: Chlorpromazine, LY294002, and wortmannin did not interfere with Cas9 transfer at concentrations where internalization of transferrin or zymosan was blocked.
source: Chlorpromazine, LY294002, and wortmannin were found not to interfere with Cas9 transfer at concentrations where the internalization of a fluorescently tagged transferrin or zymosan was blocked (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3A showing no effect on Cas9 transfer and imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D showing blocked endocytosis.

claim: siRNA knockdown of clathrin heavy chain and AP-2 subunit B1 blocked endocytosis but had only a slight effect on Cas9 transfer.
source: Furthermore, siRNA knockdown of clathrin heavy chain and AP-2 subunit B1 (validations in Figure 3—figure supplement 2) blocked endocytosis but had only a slight effect on Cas9 transfer compared to a control (Figure 3B) that dramatically blocked the uptake of transferrin by recipient cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3B showing minimal effect on Cas9 transfer and imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F showing blocked transferrin uptake.

claim: siRNA knockdown of caveolin and flotillin 2 had little effect on endocytosis of transferrin but stimulated transfer of Cas9.
source: For comparison, we also used siRNA to knockdown caveolin and flotillin 2 with little effect on endocytosis of transferrin but which stimulated transfer of Cas9 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3B showing increased Cas9 transfer and imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F showing minimal effect on transferrin uptake.

claim: Endocytosis is not necessary for Cas9/gRNA transfer.
source: Endocytosis, at least as revealed by these particular drug sensitivities and coat protein requirements, appeared not to be necessary for Cas9/gRNA transfer.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that endocytosis inhibitors and knockdowns did not block Cas9 transfer (Figure 3A-B).

claim: Latrunculin A (80 or 200 nM) and Latrunculin B (2.5 or 5 µM) substantially blocked the transfer of Cas9.
source: Lat A (80 or 200 nM) and LatB (2.5 or 5 µM) substantially blocked the transfer of Cas9 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3C demonstrating dramatic reduction in Cas9 transfer with latrunculin treatment.

claim: Actin shRNA knockdown in donor HEK293T cells reduced Cas9 transfer threefold.
source: Actin shRNA knockdown in donor HEK293T cells reduced Cas9 transfer threefold but was more effective in blocking transfer in acceptor MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3D and E), which may be because the actin knockdown efficiency was greater in MDA-MB-231 than in HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and H).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3D and E demonstrating reduced transfer with actin knockdown.

claim: Actin shRNA knockdown was more effective in blocking transfer in acceptor MDA-MB-231 cells than in donor HEK293T cells.
source: Actin shRNA knockdown in donor HEK293T cells reduced Cas9 transfer threefold but was more effective in blocking transfer in acceptor MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3D and E), which may be because the actin knockdown efficiency was greater in MDA-MB-231 than in HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and H).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3D and E and knockdown validation in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and H.

claim: Arp2/3 complex knockdown in donor but not in recipient cells reduced Cas9 transfer.
source: Arp2/3 complex knockdown in donor but not in recipient cells reduced Cas9 transfer (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3D and E demonstrating differential effects of Arp2/3 knockdown in donor vs recipient cells.

claim: The formin inhibitor SMIFH2 decreased Cas9 transfer dramatically.
source: The formin inhibitor SMIFH2 decreased Cas9 transfer dramatically (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3F demonstrating dramatic reduction in Cas9 transfer with SMIFH2 treatment.

claim: The transfer of Cas9 protein from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 depends upon actin.
source: These results suggested the transfer of Cas9 protein from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 depends upon actin and to some extent on the Arp2/3 complex or formin possibly to stabilize a cellular structure essential for intercellular traffic.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that actin depolymerization and knockdown blocked Cas9 transfer (Figure 3C-E).

claim: The transfer of Cas9 protein from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 depends to some extent on the Arp2/3 complex or formin.
source: These results suggested the transfer of Cas9 protein from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 depends upon actin and to some extent on the Arp2/3 complex or formin possibly to stabilize a cellular structure essential for intercellular traffic.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Arp2/3 knockdown and formin inhibition reduced Cas9 transfer (Figure 3D-F).

claim: Membrane tubes appearing as pseudopodia or filopodia projected from HEK293T cells made contact with MDA-MB-231 cells forming open-ended connections.
source: Membrane tubes appearing as pseudopodia or filopodia projected from HEK293T cells were seen to make contact with MDA-MB-231 cells forming what appeared to be open-ended connections (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating tubular structures connecting cells.

claim: Puncta containing endosome-related vesicles and SBP-Cas9-GFP were transported from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: On prolonged inspection, puncta containing endosome-related vesicles (labeled with streptavidin-CD63-mCherry) and SBP-Cas9-GFP were transported from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 4B), consistent with open-ended tubular connections associated with intercellular traffic.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating movement of fluorescent puncta through tubular connections.

claim: Tubular structures formed and broke during the course of visualization.
source: Such structures were seen to form and break during the course of visualization (Figure 4—video 1); however, in spite of a membrane fusion event, we did not observe wholesale cell fusion to form heterokaryons.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse video (Figure 4—video 1) showing dynamic formation and breaking of tubular connections.

claim: Wholesale cell fusion to form heterokaryons was not observed despite membrane fusion events.
source: Such structures were seen to form and break during the course of visualization (Figure 4—video 1); however, in spite of a membrane fusion event, we did not observe wholesale cell fusion to form heterokaryons.
evidence: Based on observation during live-cell imaging that cells remained separate despite tubular connections.

claim: Many thin projections termed tunneling nanotubes formed between neighboring cells.
source: At the same time, many much thinner projections, termed tunneling nanotubes, formed between neighboring cells.
evidence: Based on observation during live-cell imaging of thin tubular structures in addition to thicker connections.

claim: Open-ended tubular connections between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells were confirmed using z-stack imaging and 3D tomography.
source: The open-ended tubular connections were also observed using z-stack imaging and 3D tomography (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—videos 1 and 2), confirming the observation of open-ended tubular connections between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: Supported by 3D imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B demonstrating open-ended connections from multiple angles.

claim: Serial EM images revealed a potential point of fusion and diverse organelles populating the junction between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Serial images were stacked to reveal entire tubular connections between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells (one example in Figure 5E). A trace of the plasma membranes in connecting cells revealed a potential point of fusion and diverse organelles populating the junction between cells.
evidence: Supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 5E demonstrating membrane continuity and organelles at cell junctions.

claim: Cell junctions that appeared to convey cargo were 2 to 4 microns in diameter.
source: The cell junctions that appeared to convey cargo in these cell pairs were much thicker, from 2 to 4 microns in diameter, than the 100–200 nanometer TNTs also seen in our mixed cultures.
evidence: Based on measurement of tubular structures in EM images (Figure 5E).

claim: 8 open-ended tubular connections were found in 120 tubule-cell contacts between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Combining the live-cell imaging and CLEM results, we found 8 open-ended tubular connections in 120 tubule-cell contacts, similar to the ratio of recipient cells containing GFP signal after co-culture in the split-GFP assays (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Based on quantification of open-ended connections observed by live-cell imaging and CLEM.

claim: The ratio of open-ended connections (8 in 120) was similar to the ratio of recipient cells containing GFP signal after co-culture in the split-GFP assays.
source: Combining the live-cell imaging and CLEM results, we found 8 open-ended tubular connections in 120 tubule-cell contacts, similar to the ratio of recipient cells containing GFP signal after co-culture in the split-GFP assays (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Based on comparison of structural observations with functional transfer data from Figure 2D and E.

claim: No intercellular movement of Cas9 or GFP reporter fragments was seen in cultures of HEK293T donor and acceptor pairs.
source: Although membrane tubules were seen to emanate from HEK293T cells (Figure 4, Figure 4—video 1), no intercellular movement of Cas9 or GFP reporter fragments were seen in cultures of HEK293T donor and acceptor pairs (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on luciferase and flow cytometry data in Figure 2 showing no transfer between HEK293T cells.

claim: Tubular connections were observed between HEK293T cells, but no evidence of cytoplasmic continuity was observed.
source: Tubular connections were observed and in cases where the connections remained intact, no evidence of cytoplasmic continuity was observed (Figure 6A, Figure 6—video 1), consistent with our failure to detect Cas9 transfer between cells in a culture of HEK293T.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6A demonstrating tubular connections without cargo transfer.

claim: CLEM revealed a close-ended tubular contact between HEK293T cells.
source: Next, we evaluated HEK293 donor:acceptor cell pairs by CLEM. One such example revealed a close-ended tubular contact (Figure 6B–D), suggesting a failure in plasma membrane fusion at the tubular junction between HEK293T cells.
evidence: Supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 6B-D demonstrating lack of membrane continuity at tubular junctions.

claim: No open-ended tubular connections were found in 120 tubule-cell contacts among HEK293T cells.
source: Furthermore, combining live-cell imaging and CLEM results, we found no open-ended tubular connections in 120 tubule-cell contacts among HEK293T cells.
evidence: Based on quantification of tubular connections observed by live-cell imaging and CLEM in HEK293T-HEK293T co-cultures.

claim: Cargos were transferred through open-ended tubular connections that depend upon a plasma membrane fusion process.
source: Altogether, the above results demonstrated that cargos were transferred through open-ended tubular connections that would depend upon a plasma membrane fusion process where a fusogen catalyst may be contributed by the donor or acceptor plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that open-ended connections correlate with cargo transfer while close-ended connections do not.

claim: Syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 are endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins in humans.
source: Two examples are myomaker and myomerger for myoblast fusion, and the syncytins for trophoblast cell fusion (reviewed in Brukman et al., 2019). Syncytins are endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins: syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 in humans (Blaise et al., 2003; Frendo et al., 2003; Mi et al., 2000) and syncytin-A and -B in mice (Dupressoir et al., 2005; Peng et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Blaise et al., 2003; Frendo et al., 2003; Mi et al., 2000) establishing syncytins as retroviral envelope proteins.

claim: Syncytin-A and syncytin-B are endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins in mice.
source: Syncytins are endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins: syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 in humans (Blaise et al., 2003; Frendo et al., 2003; Mi et al., 2000) and syncytin-A and -B in mice (Dupressoir et al., 2005; Peng et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Dupressoir et al., 2005; Peng et al., 2007) establishing mouse syncytins.

claim: ASCT-2 is a receptor for syncytin-1.
source: Syncytin-mediated fusion requires complementary cell surface receptors, including ASCT-2, a widely distributed neutral amino acid transporter, a receptor for syncytin-1 (Blond et al., 2000) and Major Facilitator Superfamily Domain Containing-2 (MFSD2), a sodium-dependent lysophosphatidylcholine transporter, the receptor for syncytin-2 (Esnault et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Blond et al., 2000) identifying ASCT-2 as syncytin-1 receptor.

claim: MFSD2 is a receptor for syncytin-2.
source: Syncytin-mediated fusion requires complementary cell surface receptors, including ASCT-2, a widely distributed neutral amino acid transporter, a receptor for syncytin-1 (Blond et al., 2000) and Major Facilitator Superfamily Domain Containing-2 (MFSD2), a sodium-dependent lysophosphatidylcholine transporter, the receptor for syncytin-2 (Esnault et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Esnault et al., 2008) identifying MFSD2 as syncytin-2 receptor.

claim: Ly6e is a receptor for syncytin-A in mice.
source: In the mouse, lymphocyte antigen 6E (Ly6e) has been identified as a receptor for syncytin-A (Bacquin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Bacquin et al., 2017) identifying Ly6e as syncytin-A receptor.

claim: Syncytins are involved in the fusion of osteoclast precursors and cancer cells.
source: In addition to a role in the formation of a trophoblast syncytium during early embryonic development, syncytins are also involved in the fusion of osteoclast precursors and cancer cells (Bjerregaard et al., 2006; Uygur et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Bjerregaard et al., 2006; Uygur et al., 2019a) demonstrating syncytin roles in osteoclast and cancer cell fusion.

claim: The expression of syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 was detected in all tested cell lines.
source: First, we used immunoblotting to detect syncytins in the cell lines used in this study (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). The expression of syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 was detected in all these lines but the higher mobility, presumably furin processed form of syncytin-2, was more apparent than that of syncytin-1.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A demonstrating syncytin expression in multiple cell lines.

claim: The higher mobility, presumably furin processed form of syncytin-2, was more apparent than that of syncytin-1.
source: The expression of syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 was detected in all these lines but the higher mobility, presumably furin processed form of syncytin-2, was more apparent than that of syncytin-1.
evidence: Based on observation of protein mobility patterns in immunoblots (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

claim: MDA-MB-231 cells had a lower level of syncytin-1.
source: MDA-MB-231 cells had a lower level of syncytin-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A demonstrating reduced syncytin-1 signal in MDA-MB-231 cells.

claim: Knockdown of syncytin-1 in MDA-MB-231 cells partially decreased Cas9 transfer.
source: Knockdown of syncytin-1 in MDA-MB-231 cells partially decreased Cas9 transfer; however, knockdown of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells had a greater effect on Cas9 transfer (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–E, lane 2).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating reduced transfer with syncytin-1 knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells had a greater effect on Cas9 transfer than syncytin-1 knockdown.
source: Knockdown of syncytin-1 in MDA-MB-231 cells partially decreased Cas9 transfer; however, knockdown of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells had a greater effect on Cas9 transfer (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–E, lane 2).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating greater reduction in transfer with syncytin-2 knockdown.

claim: Expression of mouse syncytin-A partially restored Cas9 transfer in syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 knockdowns.
source: Expression of the mouse syncytin, syncytin-A, partially restored Cas9 transfer in the syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 knockdowns (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating rescue of transfer by syncytin-A expression.

claim: Full-length syncytin-A restored Cas9 transfer, but no truncated versions did.
source: As before, functional restoration of Cas9 transfer was observed by expression of full-length syncytin-A, but no significant Cas9 transfer was observed on expression of any of the syncytin-A truncated versions (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7C demonstrating rescue only with full-length syncytin-A.

claim: Expression of truncated syncytin-As reduced functional Cas9 transfer below the level achieved by knockdown of syncytin-2 alone.
source: Indeed, expression of truncated syncytin-As reduced functional Cas9 transfer below the level achieved by knockdown of syncytin-2 alone (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7C demonstrating dominant-negative effect of truncated syncytin-A.

claim: Depletion of syncytin-1 or syncytin-2 in HEK293T cells reduced functional Cas9 transfer by ~30%.
source: Next, we evaluated the effect of syncytin knockdown in HEK293T cells and found that the depletion of syncytin-1 or 2 in HEK293T reduced functional Cas9 transfer by ~30%, a much smaller effect than seen in depletion of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7D demonstrating modest reduction in transfer with syncytin knockdown in HEK293T.

claim: The effect of syncytin depletion in HEK293T cells was much smaller than the effect of syncytin-2 depletion in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Next, we evaluated the effect of syncytin knockdown in HEK293T cells and found that the depletion of syncytin-1 or 2 in HEK293T reduced functional Cas9 transfer by ~30%, a much smaller effect than seen in depletion of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Based on comparison of luciferase assay data in Figure 7A and Figure 7D showing differential effects in different cell types.

claim: Expression of syncytin-A in HEK293T cells serving as a reporter permitted some transfer of Cas9 from HEK293T donor cells.
source: The expression of syncytin-A in HEK293T cells serving as a reporter permitted some transfer of Cas9 from HEK293T cells serving as a donor (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7E demonstrating increased transfer with syncytin-A expression in HEK293T acceptor cells.

claim: The effect of syncytin-A expression in HEK293T acceptor cells was much less pronounced than when MDA-MB-231 served as acceptor cells (up to 4-fold vs. 30-fold change).
source: Although the effect was much less pronounced than when MDA-MB-231 served as acceptor cells (up to 4-fold vs. 30-fold change of Nluc/Fluc signal indicating Cas9 transfer), this result suggested that functional syncytin may be limited in HEK293T cells, thus explaining the appearance of close-ended tubular connections between HEK293T cells (Figure 6).
evidence: Based on comparison of luciferase assay data showing different magnitudes of transfer enhancement.

claim: Functional syncytin may be limited in HEK293T cells, explaining the appearance of close-ended tubular connections between HEK293T cells.
source: Although the effect was much less pronounced than when MDA-MB-231 served as acceptor cells (up to 4-fold vs. 30-fold change of Nluc/Fluc signal indicating Cas9 transfer), this result suggested that functional syncytin may be limited in HEK293T cells, thus explaining the appearance of close-ended tubular connections between HEK293T cells (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HEK293T cells form close-ended connections and have limited syncytin function.

claim: Close-ended tubular connections were observed between HEK293T cells and MDA-MB-231 syncytin-2 knockdown cells even after several hours of contact.
source: We visualized HEK293T cells containing SBP-Cas9-GFP and Myc-streptavidin-CD63-mCherry co-cultured with MDA-MB-231 syncytin-2 knockdown cells containing the Fluc:Nluc:mCherry reporter plasmid and found close-ended tubular connections even after several hours of contact (Figure 8A, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8A demonstrating persistent close-ended connections.

claim: CLEM confirmed the failure of plasma membrane fusion in conditions of syncytin-2 knockdown in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Further inspection by CLEM confirmed the failure of plasma membrane fusion in conditions of syncytin-2 knockdown in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: Supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 8B-D demonstrating lack of membrane continuity with syncytin-2 knockdown.

claim: Only one open-ended tubular connection was found in 120 tubule-cell contacts of co-cultures using MDA-MB-231 syncytin-2 knockdown cells.
source: In combining live-cell imaging and CLEM results, we found only one open-ended tubular connections in 120 tubule-cell contacts of co-cultures using MDA-MB-231 syncytin-2 knockdown cells.
evidence: Based on quantification of tubular connections observed by live-cell imaging and CLEM with syncytin-2 knockdown.

claim: Syncytin-2 is required or rate-limiting for membrane fusion at the point of contact between a tubule and the other cell plasma membrane.
source: We conclude that syncytin-2 is required or rate-limiting for membrane fusion at the point of contact between a tubule and the other cell plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that syncytin-2 knockdown dramatically reduces open-ended connections and cargo transfer.

claim: GFP-tagged syncytin-A, -1, and -2 localized in a reticular pattern within transfected cells with some label detected at or near the cell surface.
source: To further confirm the role of syncytins in membrane fusion at the site of cell-cell contact, we visualized the localization of syncytins by transient transfection of MDA-MB-231 cells with GFP-tagged forms of syncytin-A, -1, and -2. These results showed that most GFP-fusion proteins localized in a reticular pattern within transfected cells with some label detected at or near the cell surface (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C demonstrating intracellular and surface localization.

claim: Cell surface biotinylation detected full-length and furin processed forms of syncytin fusion proteins at the cell surface.
source: Syncytin-fusion proteins were immunoprecipitated with GFP antibody and SDS-PAGE blots were probed with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated streptavidin (streptavidin-HRP) and GFP antibody. HRP blots showed two species that migrated at the positions expected for full-length and furin processed forms of the syncytin fusion proteins (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by biotinylation assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D demonstrating surface-exposed syncytins.

claim: The majority of syncytin fusion protein molecules accumulated early in the secretory pathway prior to furin cleavage.
source: In contrast, immunoprecipitated fractions blotted with GFP antibody revealed species that migrated at positions expected for the full-length fusion proteins. We interpret this to mean that the majority of molecules accumulated early in the secretory pathway prior to the point of cleavage by the furin protease in the trans-Golgi membrane and beyond.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GFP blots show primarily full-length protein while biotinylation shows processed forms.

claim: Syncytin-BFP fusions were found partially localized to or near the surface and at junctions between a tubule and the adjoining cell plasma membrane.
source: Next, we visualized HEK293T cells containing SBP-Cas9-GFP and Myc-streptavidin-CD63-mCherry co-cultured with MDA-MB-231 cells containing syncytin 1-BFP (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E) or syncytin 2-BFP (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F). Syncytin-BFP fusions were found partially localized to or near the surface and at junctions between a tubule and the adjoining cell plasma membrane (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E and F demonstrating syncytin localization at cell-cell junctions.

claim: Under conditions of transient transfection, some of all three syncytins may be detected at the cell surface and in proximity to sites of membrane fusion.
source: We conclude that under conditions of transient transfection at least some of all three syncytins may be detected at the cell surface and in proximity to sites of membrane fusion.
evidence: Based on imaging and biotinylation data showing syncytin localization at cell surface and junctions.

claim: Some small fraction of the total syncytin fusion proteins experience proteolytic maturation.
source: The results of the GFP immunoblot of total proteins and biotinylation of those molecules trafficked to the cell surface suggest that some small fraction of the total fusion proteins experience proteolytic maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that biotinylated proteins show processed forms while total protein shows primarily full-length forms.

claim: MFSD2A knockdown in HEK293T cells reduced functional Cas9 transfer by approximately five- to sixfold.
source: MFSD2A knockdown in HEK293T cells reduced functional Cas9 transfer by approximately five- to sixfold (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9A demonstrating reduced transfer with MFSD2A knockdown in donor cells.

claim: MFSD2A knockdown in MDA-MB-231 acceptor cells reduced Cas9 transfer approximately three- to fourfold.
source: MFSD2A knockdown in MDA-MB-231 acceptor cells reduced Cas9 transfer approximately three- to fourfold (Figure 9C and D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9C demonstrating reduced transfer with MFSD2A knockdown in acceptor cells.

claim: MFSD2A plays roles in functional Cas9 transfer in both HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: These results suggested roles for MFSD2A in functional Cas9 transfer in both HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MFSD2A knockdown reduces transfer in both cell types (Figure 9A and C).

claim: Syncytin and its receptor play roles in intercellular transfer among MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Given the above results reveal that cargos could be transferred among MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 2G), the data in Figure 9 suggest that syncytin and its receptor may also play roles in the intercellular transfer among MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MDA-MB-231 cells can transfer cargo to themselves and that syncytin/MFSD2A affect transfer.

claim: MFSD2A localizes to the cell surface.
source: Finally, we used IF and live-cell imaging and localized MFSD2A to the cell surface of normal and GFP-MFSD2A-transfected cells (Figure 9E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 9E and F demonstrating MFSD2A at cell surface.

claim: Exosomes are internalized by reporter cells but do not efficiently deliver functional Cas9 protein to the nucleus.
source: We found that EVs are internalized by reporter cells but do not efficiently deliver functional Cas9 protein to the nucleus.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing exosome internalization (Figure 1H) but minimal gene editing (Figure 1F).

claim: Donor and acceptor cells co-cultured to permit cell contact resulted in highly effective transfer.
source: In contrast, donor and acceptor cells co-cultured to permit cell contact resulted in a highly effective transfer.
evidence: Based on luciferase assay data showing up to 60-fold increase in signal with cell-cell contact (Figure 2A).

claim: HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 recorded optimal intercellular transfer among tested donor and acceptor cell pairs.
source: Among our tested donor and acceptor cell pairs, HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 recorded optimal intercellular transfer.
evidence: Based on comparison of different cell pair combinations showing highest transfer with HEK293T-MDA-MB-231 (Figure 2A).

claim: Depolymerization of F-actin greatly decreased Cas9 transfer.
source: Depolymerization of F-actin greatly decreased Cas9 transfer, whereas inhibitors of endocytosis or knockdown of genes implicated in this process had little effect on transfer.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing latrunculin treatment blocks transfer (Figure 3C) while endocytosis inhibitors do not (Figure 3A-B).

claim: Inhibitors of endocytosis or knockdown of genes implicated in endocytosis had little effect on Cas9 transfer.
source: Depolymerization of F-actin greatly decreased Cas9 transfer, whereas inhibitors of endocytosis or knockdown of genes implicated in this process had little effect on transfer.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing endocytosis inhibitors and knockdowns do not block transfer (Figure 3A-B).

claim: Intercellular transfer of cargos occurred through open-ended membrane tubular connections.
source: Imaging results suggest that intercellular transfer of cargos occurred through open-ended membrane tubular connections.
evidence: Based on live-cell imaging and CLEM data showing open-ended connections correlating with cargo transfer (Figures 4-5).

claim: Cultures consisting only of HEK293T cells form close-ended tubular connections ineffective in cargo transfer.
source: In contrast, cultures consisting only of HEK293T cells form close-ended tubular connections ineffective in cargo transfer.
evidence: Based on imaging data showing close-ended connections in HEK293T-HEK293T pairs (Figure 6) and lack of functional transfer (Figure 2).

claim: Depletion of human endogenous fusogens, syncytins, especially syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells, significantly reduced Cas9 transfer.
source: Depletion of human endogenous fusogens, syncytins, especially syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells, significantly reduced Cas9 transfer.
evidence: Based on luciferase assay data showing dramatic reduction in transfer with syncytin-2 knockdown (Figure 7A).

claim: Full-length mouse syncytin rescued the effect of depletion of human syncytins on Cas9 transfer.
source: Full-length mouse syncytin, but not truncated mutants, rescued the effect of depletion of human syncytins on Cas9 transfer.
evidence: Based on luciferase assay data showing rescue of transfer by full-length syncytin-A but not truncated versions (Figure 7C).

claim: Truncated mouse syncytin mutants did not rescue the effect of depletion of human syncytins on Cas9 transfer.
source: Full-length mouse syncytin, but not truncated mutants, rescued the effect of depletion of human syncytins on Cas9 transfer.
evidence: Based on luciferase assay data showing no rescue by truncated syncytin-A versions (Figure 7C).

claim: Mouse syncytin overexpression in HEK293T cells partially facilitated Cas9 transfer among HEK293T cells.
source: Mouse syncytin overexpression in HEK293T cells partially facilitated Cas9 transfer among HEK293T cells.
evidence: Based on luciferase assay data showing modest increase in transfer with syncytin-A expression in HEK293T acceptor cells (Figure 7E).

claim: Syncytin may serve as the fusogen responsible for the formation of an open-ended connection between cells.
source: These findings suggest that syncytin may serve as the fusogen responsible for the formation of an open-ended connection between cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that syncytin depletion reduces open-ended connections and transfer, while syncytin expression rescues transfer.
